title: The list of installed software is damaged
what: The database that remembers which software is installed cannot be read, so updates and installs will fail.
why: It can be damaged by a power cut during an update.
fix_summary: Rebuild the list of installed software from the files on the disk. Your files and settings are not touched.
backup_first: A copy of the software database.
undo: The copy is kept in the repair backup folder.
manual: Run: sudo rpm --rebuilddb

title: An install or update was cut off half-way
what: Some software is only partly installed, because an update was interrupted.
why: Partly installed software can break other programs and block updates.
fix_summary: Finish the interrupted install and fix broken packages. Needs the internet.
undo: Not needed: this only finishes what was started.
manual: Run: sudo dpkg --configure -a && sudo apt-get -f install

title: An update was cut off and left two versions of some software
what: {detail}
why: Duplicate versions confuse the update tool and can break programs.
fix_summary: Remove the old duplicates and finish the update. Needs the internet.
undo: Not needed: this only removes leftovers.
manual: Run: sudo dnf remove --duplicates

title: Some software needs something that is missing
what: {detail}
why: Broken links between packages make installs and updates fail.
fix_summary: Fix broken package links. It shows what it will do and needs the internet.
manual: Run: sudo dnf distro-sync (Fedora) or sudo apt-get -f install (Debian)

title: Some software is on hold and will not update
what: {detail}
why: Held software misses security updates.
fix_summary: Nothing is changed automatically, since a hold is usually deliberate.
manual: Release a hold with: sudo apt-mark unhold NAME

title: Some background services failed to start
what: {detail}
why: A failed service can mean a feature, like printing or Bluetooth, does not work.
fix_summary: Clear the failed marks and try to start each failed service once. Nothing is deleted.
manual: Run: systemctl --failed, then: systemctl restart NAME

title: Some Flatpak apps are damaged
what: {detail}
why: Damaged app files can stop apps from opening.
fix_summary: Repair Flatpak apps and remove unused parts. Needs the internet.
manual: Run: flatpak repair --system

title: Too many system snapshots are using space
what: There are {detail} snapshots (earlier copies of the system). They take up disk space.
why: Snapshots pile up and can fill the disk.
fix_summary: Remove old snapshots following the usual rules, keeping the recent ones.
undo: Old snapshots cannot be brought back.
manual: Run: sudo snapper -c root cleanup number

title: Old downloads are taking a lot of space
what: Software downloads and caches use about {detail} MB.
why: They are only needed once; clearing them frees space.
fix_summary: Delete downloaded package files and old logs. Your files are not touched.
undo: Not needed: they are downloaded again if needed.
manual: Run: sudo dnf clean all

title: The system logs have grown very large
what: The logs use about {detail} MB of the disk.
why: They fill space and slow down some tools.
fix_summary: Trim the logs to a sensible size. Recent entries are kept.
undo: Old log entries cannot be brought back.
manual: Run: sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M

title: Software nobody needs is still installed
what: About {detail} packages are no longer needed by anything.
why: They take space and need updates.
fix_summary: Remove unused packages. It shows the list first and asks again.
undo: Install any of them again from the software sources.
manual: Run: sudo dnf autoremove (or apt autoremove)

title: An important software source is switched off
what: One of the main software sources is switched off, so you do not get updates from it.
why: Without it, security updates stop arriving.
fix_summary: Switch the main software sources back on.
backup_first: A copy of the source files.
undo: The copies are in the repair backup folder.
manual: Edit the file in /etc/yum.repos.d/ and set enabled=1.

title: Updates cannot be downloaded
what: The update tool recently reported problems downloading lists of updates.
why: You may have no internet, or a software source address is out of date.
fix_summary: Open the software repair helper.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
undo: The helper explains how to undo.
manual: Check your internet, then run: sudo dnf clean all && sudo dnf makecache

title: The clock is not being kept right by the internet
what: Automatic time setting is not working, so the clock can drift.
why: A wrong clock breaks secure websites, updates and logins.
fix_summary: Switch on automatic time setting and sync the clock now.
manual: Run: sudo timedatectl set-ntp true

title: Firmware updates are waiting
what: {detail}
why: Firmware updates fix bugs and security problems in the BIOS, SSD, dock or other parts.
fix_summary: Install the firmware updates. Plug in the charger first; some need a restart.
undo: Firmware updates cannot be undone; they are signed by the maker.
manual: Open Discover > Updates, or run: sudo fwupdmgr update

title: The security system has blocked a lot of actions
what: About {detail} actions were blocked by the security system (SELinux) since start-up.
why: It may be blocking a program that has a legitimate need, or a malicious attempt.
fix_summary: Nothing is changed automatically.
manual: Run: sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent, or open the SELinux alert tool.

title: The security system is switched off or only warns
what: SELinux is not enforcing, so it only reports problems and does not block them.
why: It is a main layer of protection against damage from compromised programs.
fix_summary: Turning it on needs a full relabel at restart. Not done automatically.
manual: Set SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config, run: sudo touch /.autorelabel and restart.

title: A restart is needed to finish updates
what: Updates were installed that only take effect after a restart.
why: Until you restart, the old versions are still running.
fix_summary: Nothing is restarted automatically, because it could lose your work.
manual: Save your work and restart the computer.

title: The computer has not been updated for a long time
what: The last update was about {detail} days ago.
why: Updates fix security holes. Old systems are an easy target.
fix_summary: Install all updates. Needs the internet; some updates need a restart.
backup_first: A snapshot is taken first if available.
undo: Roll back from the snapshot list if something goes wrong.
manual: Open Discover > Updates, or run: sudo dnf upgrade --refresh (or apt upgrade)

title: The firewall is switched off
what: The firewall, which blocks unwanted connections from the network, is not running.
why: Without it, services on your computer may be reachable by others on the same network.
fix_summary: Switch the firewall on with the usual safe settings. Normal use is not affected.
manual: Run: sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld (or sudo ufw enable)

title: Remote access (SSH) is open to anyone on the network
what: The computer accepts remote logins with a password from the whole network.
why: Attackers constantly try common passwords on open SSH.
fix_summary: Switch off remote access. Switch it back on later if you really need it.
manual: Run: sudo systemctl disable --now sshd. Or keep it and allow only key logins.

title: New passwords may be too short
what: The rules for new passwords allow very short ones.
why: Short passwords are easy to guess.
fix_summary: Require at least 10 characters for new passwords. Existing passwords are not changed.
backup_first: A copy of the rules file.
undo: The copy is kept next to the file.
manual: Edit /etc/security/pwquality.conf and set minlen = 10

title: There have been many failed sign-in attempts
what: About {detail} failed sign-ins were recorded since start-up.
why: It could be someone guessing your password, or you mistyping.
fix_summary: Nothing is changed automatically.
manual: If you did not cause them, turn off remote access and change your password.

title: No virus scan for a long time
what: A virus scan has not been done for a while.
why: Regular scans catch files that arrived by email, USB sticks or downloads.
fix_summary: Open the virus scan helper. Nothing is deleted without your say-so.
manual: Choose Scan for viruses in the repair menu.

title: No recovery key for your encrypted disk
what: Your disk is encrypted but no spare recovery key has been saved.
why: If you forget the disk password, the files cannot be recovered at all.
fix_summary: Make a recovery key and show it once so you can print or write it down.
backup_first: Nothing is changed on your files.
undo: The key can be removed with the recovery key tool.
manual: Run: secure-linux-recovery-key create and keep the key somewhere safe, not on this computer.

title: You have no backups set up
what: Nothing is copying your files to another place.
why: If this computer is lost, stolen or breaks, your files are gone.
fix_summary: Backups need you to choose where to put them.
manual: Plug in a USB drive or choose the home server in the backup settings.

title: Your last backup is old
what: Your files have not been backed up for a while.
why: Anything new since then would be lost if the computer failed today.
fix_summary: Plug in your backup drive and run a backup.
manual: Plug in your backup drive or connect to the home network, then back up.

title: Your laptop's disk is not encrypted
what: The disk is not locked with a password, so anyone with the laptop can read your files.
why: Laptops get lost and stolen. Encryption keeps your files private.
fix_summary: Disk encryption cannot be turned on safely afterwards.
manual: Back up and reinstall with disk encryption on, when convenient.

title: Forgotten your login password?
what: If you cannot sign in, you can reset the Linux login password from this rescue system.
why: You still need the disk password (or the recovery key) if the disk is encrypted.
fix_summary: Open the password helper. It asks which account first.
backup_first: Nothing is changed until you choose.
manual: Choose Forgot my Linux login password in the repair menu.

title: An account is locked after too many wrong passwords
what: An account has had several wrong password attempts and may be locked for a few minutes.
why: The lock protects against password guessing and clears by itself after a while.
fix_summary: Clear the wrong-password count so you can sign in again.
manual: Run: sudo faillock --user NAME --reset

title: Administrator access is not working
what: {detail}
why: Without it you cannot install software or fix problems from your account.
fix_summary: Fix the administrator settings and make sure your account is an administrator.
undo: The copy is kept next to the file.
manual: From the rescue stick, add your user to the wheel group and fix /etc/sudoers.

title: Sign-in keeps failing because of file ownership
what: {detail}
why: When important files in your home folder belong to the administrator, you can be thrown back to the login screen.
fix_summary: Give the files in your home folder back to you. Only ownership changes; nothing is deleted.
backup_first: A list of what is changed.
undo: The list lets you put ownership back.
manual: From a terminal: sudo chown -R USER:USER /home/USER
